prompt: Explain in practical terms why an operating system scheduler tries to balance throughput, latency, and fairness. Give one concrete CPU scheduling example.

A small engineering team is optimizing CPU inference for a transformer model on an eight-core RISC-V system. The model uses OpenMP workers, vector instructions, shared barriers, and a key-value cache. Requests arrive independently, and prompt processing may overlap with token generation from older requests. Explain how CPU contention, worker wakeups, cache locality, barrier laggards, and thread migration can affect time to first token and steady-state token throughput. Then propose a careful measurement method that separates application behavior from scheduler effects. Use clear technical language and state any assumptions.

Consider a server with eight identical CPU cores and two independent language-model processes. Each process creates eight OpenMP compute workers and serves four concurrent streaming requests. All workers may execute RISC-V vector instructions. Prompt processing builds a computation graph over many input tokens, while decoding repeatedly evaluates a graph for the next token. Graph nodes contain parallel work followed by barriers, and some nodes expose less parallelism than others. The operating system sees runnable threads, sleeping threads, wakeups, CPU affinity, and execution history, but it does not automatically know model phases or graph boundaries.

The first model is already decoding when requests for the second model arrive. A scheduler must decide whether to preserve the incumbent model's cache locality, rapidly serve the new model's prompt work, divide CPU time fairly between the two worker teams, or temporarily favor one team so that its workers reach barriers together. Long time slices can reduce involuntary preemption but cannot prevent workers from sleeping at application barriers. Strict core partitioning avoids interference but can waste cores when one model has insufficient parallel work. A work-conserving gang policy may improve coordination, but an aggressive implementation can starve kernel work or increase queueing delay.

Write a structured technical analysis of this scenario. Distinguish throughput, time to first token, inter-token latency, fairness, CPU service time, runqueue delay, context switches, and vector context handling. Explain which metrics should be collected from streaming responses and which should come from the kernel. Identify at least three misleading measurements and show how a deterministic benchmark can avoid them. Finish with acceptance criteria for comparing a shared-core scheduler against a four-core-per-model spatial partition.

You are reviewing an experiment on a fanless eight-core RISC-V development board. Two independent llama.cpp servers load the same quantized model. Each server uses four parallel request slots, eight generation threads, eight batch threads, ordinary CPU execution, and a context budget shared by its slots. The experiment is intended to reveal operating-system scheduling effects when two OpenMP worker teams compete for the same CPUs. Every response is streamed. Sampling temperature is zero, the random seed is fixed, end-of-sequence stopping is disabled, and each request must emit exactly the configured number of tokens.

Four incumbent requests are submitted one second apart to the first server. Their prompts have different fixed lengths. The benchmark watches actual token events rather than sleeping for a guessed duration. Only after all four incumbent requests have emitted a fixed milestone number of tokens does it submit four requests to the second server, also one second apart. This creates a repeatable overlap between incumbent decoding and newly injected prompt processing. A reverse run swaps the two server roles so that port order, process start order, and warm cache effects can be detected. Each complete experiment repeats both directions several times.

The client records the monotonic send time, first-token time, every token arrival time, final-token time, token identifiers, completion status, and server timing metadata. From these events it computes time to first token, end-to-end latency, decode throughput, inter-token latency percentiles, aggregate goodput, and the incumbent model's inter-token degradation after injection. During the interval when both models have outstanding work, it also computes each model's observed token rate and Jain's fairness index. Because only four injected requests exist in one run, the report does not pretend that a per-run p95 is statistically strong; it pools equivalent samples across valid repetitions.

A low-priority board-side sampler reads each server thread's schedstat, context-switch counters, migration count, CPU frequency, thermal zones, and memory state once per second. It does not continuously trace every futex or stack in the default performance run. An optional diagnostic profile records RISC-V vector save and restore candidates for each process. Kernel logs and sched_ext state are captured before and after every run so watchdog fallback, stalls, out-of-memory events, or thermal invalidation cannot silently enter an average.

There are several important controls. In the shared-core control, both servers use all eight cores and eight compute workers. In the spatial control, each server is restricted to a disjoint group of four cores and uses four workers. Services are restarted for every run, all request slots are warmed, prompt caching is disabled, and prompt token counts are checked through the model tokenizer. A run is invalid if any request times out, emits the wrong number of tokens, starts before its required milestone, changes deterministic output, triggers a kernel scheduling failure, or loses a server process.

Analyze this benchmark as if you were the engineer responsible for deciding whether a new multi-model scheduler is worth implementing. Explain the expected behavior of CFS in both controls, the tradeoff between work conservation and spatial isolation, how prefill interference can appear in incumbent inter-token latency, why aggregate throughput alone can hide starvation, and why CPU runtime fairness is not identical to token-rate fairness. Discuss how prompt length changes prefill demand without changing the fixed decode work. Describe how paired forward and reverse runs reduce systematic bias. Finally, propose a concise decision rule that considers injected-request latency, incumbent disruption, aggregate throughput, fairness, stability, and kernel safety together instead of selecting a scheduler from a single best sample.
